You've just eliminated hardcoded credentials, one of the most critical security patterns in cloud
engineering. Instead of storing permanent access keys that could be stolen, leaked to GitHub,
or extracted from compromised servers, you used a role that provides temporary, auto-rotating
credentials valid only for that specific EC2 instance. You also implemented least privilege: your
application can read from one S3 bucket but cannot delete files, access other buckets, or touch
any other AWS services. If an attacker exploits your application, the damage is contained to
exactly what that role permits, nothing more.
This same pattern applies everywhere: Lambda functions accessing DynamoDB, ECS
containers reading secrets, and CI/CD pipelines deploying applications. Every time you're
tempted to create access keys, ask yourself, "Could I use a role instead?" The answer is almost
always yes, and your security will be dramatically better for it.
IAM controls who can access your resources, but what about controlling what can reach them
over the network? An attacker with stolen credentials is one threat, but what about attackers
scanning the internet for exposed databases or trying to exploit vulnerable services? This is
where network idx_94338930 security comes in, and it's just as critical as identity management.

85562.title: clouddevopsengineersguide
85562.heading: Chapter 12 224
85562.content:
Chapter 12 224
Implementing network security with VPCs and
security groups
Controlling who can access your resources with IAM is one half of the security equation. The
other half is controlling what can access your resources over the network. In AWS, this is
primarily managed idx_d4bf2bb6 through Virtual Private Clouds (VPCs). A VPC is your own logically
isolated section of the AWS cloud, a private digital network that you define and control. It's the
foundational building block for your cloud architecture, your digital fortress.
Understanding VPCs: Your private network in the cloud
Think of a VPC like idx_4200980c owning a private office building in a massive business district (the AWS
region). While AWS owns and operates the entire district with all its infrastructure, your VPC is
your private floor or building within it, completely isolated from other tenants. You control
everything about your space: the layout, the security checkpoints, who can enter, and how
different rooms connect to each other.
When you create a VPC, you define its IP address range using CIDR notation (such as
10.0.0.0/16), which determines how many IP addresses are available for your resources. You
then divide this space into subnets, or idx_64aa6b9f smaller network segments that can be placed in
different availability zones for redundancy. This is like dividing your office building into
different floors or departments.
Public versus private subnets: Controlling internet access
Subnets come in two fundamental types, each serving different security purposes:
Public subnets have a route to an internet gateway, allowing resources within them to
idx_6d0b6773 communicate directly with the internet. This is where you place resources that need to
be publicly accessible, such as web servers, load balancers, or bastion hosts. Think of
this as your building's lobby; it's designed to interact with the outside world.
Private subnets have no direct route to the internet, making resources within them
completely idx_d61df4f2 isolated from inbound internet traffic. This is where you place your
databases, application servers, and any sensitive workloads. These resources can still
reach the internet for updates or API calls through a NAT gateway (which allows
outbound traffic only), but they cannot be reached from the internet. This is like your
building's secure server room; employees inside can make phone calls out, but no one
from outside can call in.
Now that we understand how VPCs establish your overarching network boundaries and
security groups enforce your granular access rules, let's look at how they combine to secure a
classic, real-world deployment.
•
•
225 Advanced Cloud Security and Identity Management
Security groups: Your software firewall
While VPCs provide network isolation at the infrastructure level, security groups act as virtual

85563.title: clouddevopsengineersguide
85563.heading: Chapter 12 224
85563.content:
firewalls that control traffic at the individual resource level, specifically, at the network
interface of each EC2 instance, RDS database, or Lambda function.
Security groups operate on a simple but powerful principle: deny all by default, allow
explicitly. When you create a security group, it starts by blocking all inbound traffic and
allowing all outbound traffic. You then add specific rules to allow only the traffic you need.
Here's what makes security groups idx_a96fcfb1 particularly powerful:
Stateful operation: If you allow inbound traffic on port 443 (HTTPS), the response
traffic is automatically allowed back out; you don't need to create a separate outbound
rule. Security groups track connections and understand that response traffic belongs to
an allowed request.
Rule structure: Each rule specifies the following:
Type: The protocol (TCP, UDP, or ICMP) and port range
Source/Destination: Where traffic can come from (for inbound) or go to (for
outbound)
Description: What this rule is for (always document your rules!)
Source flexibility: Instead of just IP addresses, you can reference other security groups.
This creates dynamic, maintainable security policies. For example, your database
security group can allow inbound traffic from WebServerSecurityGroup rather than
specific IP addresses. When you add or remove web servers, the database automatically
allows or denies their traffic; no manual rule updates are needed.
Three-tier web application
Here's how VPCs and security groups idx_b2c6b932 work together in a typical architecture:
VPC: 10.0.0.0/16 (your entire private network)
Public subnet (10.0.1.0/24): Contains a load balancer:
Security group: Allow inbound HTTPS (443) from anywhere (0.0.0.0/0); allow
outbound to WebServerSecurityGroup

85564.content:
Chapter 12 226
Private subnet 1 (10.0.2.0/24): Contains web application servers:
Security group: Allow inbound traffic only from LoadBalancerSecurityGroup;
allow outbound to DatabaseSecurityGroup
Private subnet 2 (10.0.3.0/24): Contains RDS database:
Security group: Allow inbound traffic only from WebServerSecurityGroup on
port 3306 (MySQL); deny all outbound except for responses
Notice the layered defense: the database is in a private subnet (no internet access), and its
security group only accepts connections from the web servers. Even if an attacker somehow
compromises the load idx_707c5e37 balancer, they cannot directly reach the database; they'd need to
compromise a web server first. This is defense in depth.
Now that you understand the theory of how VPCs and security groups create layered security,
let's dive deeper into the actual components that make this isolation possible. Understanding
subnets, gateways, and routing is essential for architecting secure networks; these are the
building blocks you'll use to construct every cloud environment you deploy.
Building your fortress: VPCs, subnets, and gateways
Within your VPC, you create subnets, which are smaller, segmented ranges of IP addresses.
This is how you divide your fortress into different security zones. The key distinction is
between public and private subnets. A subnet becomes "public" only if its traffic is routed to an
internet gateway, which is the component that allows communication between your VPC and
the public internet. A "private" subnet, by contrast, has no such route, making its resources
inaccessible from the outside world.
Let's see how this works in practice with a real e-commerce application.
Use case: E-commerce platform architecture
You're building a platform that idx_aacd24f9 serves thousands of customers, processes payments, and stores
sensitive user data.
This is the setup:
VPC: 10.0.0.0/16 (your entire private network space)
Public subnet (10.0.1.0/24) in us-east-1a: Contains your Application Load Balancer
and a bastion host
Private subnet 1 (10.0.2.0/24) in us-east-1a: Contains web application servers (EC2
instances running your Node.js/Python app)
Private subnet 2 (10.0.3.0/24) in us-east-1b: Contains your RDS PostgreSQL
database and ElastiCache Redis cluster
•
◦
•
◦
•
•
•
•
227 Advanced Cloud Security and Identity Management
Why this architecture?
The Application Load Balancer idx_254645fd sits in the public subnet with a route to the internet gateway. It
needs to receive HTTPS requests from customers browsing your website. Your web servers are
in a private subnet with no direct internet access. They receive traffic only from the load
balancer through internal routing within the VPC. When your application needs to call
external APIs (such as a payment processor or shipping service), outbound requests go through

85565.title: clouddevopsengineersguide
85565.heading: Chapter 12 226
85565.content:
a NAT gateway placed in the public subnet. The NAT gateway allows your private servers to
initiate outbound connections while preventing any inbound connections from the internet.
Your database is in an even more isolated private subnet. It has no route to the internet at all,
not even through a NAT gateway. The database only accepts connections from your application
servers within the VPC. This means that even if an attacker somehow obtains your database
credentials, they cannot connect to it from outside your AWS environment. The only way to
reach the database is by first compromising an application server or using the bastion host (a
hardened, tightly monitored jump server in the public subnet that administrators use for
maintenance).
The security impact
This layered architecture idx_6bd7bab9 means that a vulnerability in your web application (such as a SQL
injection flaw or remote code execution bug) doesn't automatically expose your database to
the internet. An attacker would need to do the following:
Exploit the web application.
Pivot from the compromised web server to the database subnet.
Authenticate to the database (which uses different credentials and ideally IAM
database authentication).
Each layer adds friction and detection opportunities. Your CloudTrail logs, VPC Flow Logs, and
GuardDuty monitoring can catch unusual network patterns, such as a web server suddenly
trying to scan the database subnet or an application server making unexpected outbound
connections.
With your VPC divided into public and private zones through subnets and gateways, you've
established the perimeter of your fortress. But controlling what enters and leaves each zone
requires more granular tools, two types of firewalls that work at different layers to enforce your
security policies.

85567.title: clouddevopsengineersguide
85567.heading: Chapter 12 228
85567.content:
Chapter 12 228
Security groups versus NACLs: The guards at the gates
To control the flow of traffic to and from your resources, you have two types of firewalls:
Security groups (SGs): These idx_043d3112 are the most common and versatile. An SG acts as a
virtual firewall at the instance level. It's like a security guard assigned to the door of each
individual server. SGs are stateful, which is a crucial feature. This means if you allow
an inbound connection (e.g., an HTTP request from a user), the corresponding
outbound connection (the web page being sent back to the user) is automatically
allowed, regardless of your outbound rules. You only need to define the "allow" rules.
Network access control lists (NACLs): These are an optional layer of security that acts
as a firewall idx_158cfd42 at the subnet level. They are the guards at the main gate of a whole section
of your fortress. NACLs are stateless. This means you must explicitly define rules for
both inbound and outbound traffic. If you allow inbound traffic on port 80, you must
also create a corresponding outbound rule to allow the return traffic. Because of this
complexity, most network security is managed with SGs, while NACLs are used for
broader, subnet-level rules, such as blocking a known malicious IP address from an
entire subnet.
A common and secure architecture is to create a multi-tier environment within your VPC. You
place your web servers in a public subnet. The security group for these servers would allow
inbound traffic on port 443 (HTTPS) from anywhere (0.0.0.0/0). You then place your
databases in a private subnet. The security group for the database would be configured to only
allow inbound traffic on the database port (e.g., 3306) from the security group ID of your web
servers. This powerful feature ensures that only your application servers can talk to your
database, and the database is completely inaccessible from the public internet.
You've built multiple defense layers: IAM controls who accesses resources, and VPCs and
security groups control network traffic. But what if an attacker bypasses these controls,
through physical access to a backup, intercepted traffic, or a zero-day exploit? Your final,
essential defense is encryption.
Encrypting data at rest and in transit
The final layer of idx_2a25c410 defense is encryption. Even if an unauthorized user somehow gains access to
your storage, encryption ensures that the data they see is just unintelligible gibberish. There
are two critical states where data must be protected:
Encryption in transit: This protects your data as it travels over a network. Think of it
as sending a idx_0c00bda2 message in a sealed, tamper-proof envelope. The primary technology for
this idx_02386a58 is Transport Layer Security (TLS), which is the protocol that powers HTTPS. You

85568.title: clouddevopsengineersguide
85568.heading: Chapter 12 228
85568.content:
•
•
•
229 Advanced Cloud Security and Identity Management
should always configure your applications to use TLS for all communication, both
externally with users and internally between microservices. AWS services such as
Elastic Load Balancing make it easy to terminate TLS at the load balancer, simplifying
certificate management for your applications.
Encryption at rest: This idx_acd847e6 protects your data when it's stored on disk, like locking the
contents of a file before you save it to your hard drive. AWS makes enabling encryption
at rest incredibly simple, primarily through the AWS Key Management Service
(KMS). KMS is a managed service that makes it easy for you to create and idx_6535fa58 control the
encryption keys used to encrypt your data. When you create an S3 bucket, an EBS
volume for an EC2 instance, or an RDS database, there is a simple checkbox to enable
encryption. When you check this box, AWS uses KMS to manage the keys and
transparently handle the encryption and decryption of your data without you having to
manage the complex cryptography yourself. It is a security best practice to enable
encryption at rest for all your stored data.
By implementing both encryption in transit and at rest, you've created a comprehensive
defense where data is protected throughout its entire lifecycle, whether it's moving between
services, sitting in a database, or stored in backups. This encryption layer works in concert with
your IAM policies and network security to ensure that even if an attacker bypasses your other
defenses, they're left with encrypted data they cannot read. Together, these three pillars,
identity and access management, network security, and encryption, form the foundation of a
secure cloud architecture.
Three additional practices strengthen this layered posture at the account level. First, enforce
MFA on every IAM user. An MFA enforcement policy attached to your users can deny all actions
except setting up an MFA device until the user has enrolled, making MFA mandatory rather
than optional. Second, in the S3 console, enable Block Public Access settings for this
account. This account-level toggle overrides any individual bucket configuration that would
make a bucket publicly readable, acting as a safety net against accidental data exposure. Third,
if your organization manages multiple AWS accounts, AWS Organizations with SCPs adds a
governance ceiling above individual account IAM policies. An SCP applied at the organizational
unit level can prevent any administrator in any child account from disabling CloudTrail,
removing S3 Block Public Access, or creating overly permissive IAM policies, regardless of their
account-level permissions. Together, MFA enforcement, S3 Block Public Access, and SCPs
complement the IAM, VPC, and encryption controls already in place, giving you defense in

85569.title: clouddevopsengineersguide
85569.heading: Chapter 12 228
85569.content:
depth at the identity, network, data, and governance layers simultaneously.
•

85570.title: clouddevopsengineersguide
85570.heading: Chapter 12 230
85570.content:
Chapter 12 230
Summary
This chapter elevated your security expertise from application-level concerns to the
foundational security of your entire cloud infrastructure. You learned the Shared Responsibility
Model, the critical framework defining what AWS secures (physical infrastructure, hardware,
and hypervisor) versus what you must secure (data, applications, configurations, and access
controls). Understanding this boundary is essential: 99% of cloud security failures stem from
customer misconfiguration, not provider vulnerabilities.
You then learned about AWS IAM, the central control system for cloud security. Through the
core components of users, groups, policies, and roles, you learned to implement the principle
of least privilege. In hands-on practice, you created a secure IAM role allowing an EC2 instance
to access S3 without hardcoded credentials, eliminating one of the most common cloud
security vulnerabilities by using temporary, auto-rotating credentials instead of permanent
access keys.
Moving beyond identity, you explored network security through VPCs and security groups. You
learned to architect defense in depth by dividing infrastructure into public and private subnets,
controlling traffic with internet gateways and NAT gateways, and applying security groups as
stateful firewalls. A real-world e-commerce example showed how proper VPC architecture
ensures that compromising one layer doesn't automatically expose databases or sensitive
workloads.
Finally, you implemented encryption as your last defense layer: TLS protecting data in transit,
and AWS KMS providing simple encryption at rest. Together with IAM and network security,
these three pillars ensure that even if attackers bypass other defenses, they face unreadable
encrypted data.
Your cloud infrastructure is now automated, observable, and fundamentally secure with
layered defenses against stolen credentials, network intrusions, and data breaches. In the next
chapter, we'll focus on system maintenance and reliability, ensuring that your secure
infrastructure stays healthy, performant, and available even as it scales and evolves.

Chapter 12 232
13
System Maintenance and
Reliability
You have built an impressive software factory. Your pipelines are automated, secure, and
observable. You can ship code from a developer's laptop to production with speed and
confidence. But a new, nagging question begins to surface, often late at night: What happens
when things break? A server crashes, a network cable is cut, or an entire data center goes
offline. All the automation in the world is meaningless if the underlying system is fragile.
Speed without reliability is a liability.
This chapter is about building systems that last. We will move from the speed of deployment to
the resilience of the deployed system. You will learn the language of reliability engineering,
defining what "uptime" actually means idx_653053f0 with Service-Level Objectives (SLOs) and Service-
Level Agreements (SLAs). We'll architect for failure by exploring idx_602df730 high-availability and fault-
tolerant patterns that can withstand common outages. You will get hands-on experience with
implementing the cornerstone of idx_b14d50f6 cloud resilience: a self-healing architecture idx_72b42872 using an
Application Load Balancer (ALB) and an Auto-Scaling Group (ASG). We will then expand
our view to plan for larger-scale events idx_3f0ddcf7 with Disaster Recovery (DR) strategies.
In this chapter, we're going to cover the following main topics:
Defining SLIs, SLAs, and SLOs
High-availability and fault-tolerant architectures
Hands-on: Building a self-healing system with an auto-scaling group
Disaster recovery planning and execution
•
•
•
•
Technical requirements
This chapter's hands-on exercise requires an active AWS account, with the Free Tier being
sufficient. You will need permissions to create and manage ALBs, target groups, EC2 launch
templates, and ASGs. The AWS CLI should be installed and configured on your local machine
for testing and verification.
You can download the example project and code for this book by following the instructions in
the Download the example code files section in the Preface of this book.
This chapter's code files are included in the downloadable code bundle.
Defining SLIs, SLOs, and SLAs
Before we can build a reliable system, we must first define what "reliable" means. Simply
aiming for "100% uptime" is not only practically impossible but also an unhelpful goal. True
reliability engineering is a practice of trade-offs, balancing the cost of reliability with the needs
of the business and the expectations of the users. We achieve this clarity through a hierarchy of
precise definitions: SLIs, SLOs, and SLAs.
The hierarchy of reliability
These three idx_bd519808 concepts form a hierarchy because each one builds upon and constrains the next,
flowing from raw measurement at the bottom to customer-facing promises at the top. Think of

85572.title: clouddevopsengineersguide
85572.heading: Chapter 12 232
85572.content:
a pizza delivery service that wants to be known for its speed:
Service-Level Indicator (SLI): This idx_ce7b8166 is the foundation, the raw measurement. It's a
quantifiable metric of the service being provided. For our pizza service, a good SLI
would be the delivery time for each order. For a web service, common SLIs are request
latency, error rate, or system throughput. Choosing the right SLI is critical; it must be a
true reflection of the user experience. Without accurate SLIs, you're building on sand;
you can't set meaningful goals if you're measuring the wrong thing.
SLO: This is the idx_19989250 internal goal built on top of your SLI. It's a target value for an SLI that
you aim to meet over a specific period. Our pizza service might set an SLO that 99% of
all deliveries (the SLI) in a month must be completed in under 30 minutes. An SLO is
your internal benchmark for success, which is ambitious but achievable, and it drives
your engineering decisions. For a web service, an SLO might be "99.9% of successful
API calls will complete in under 200 ms." The SLO sits above the SLI because it
transforms raw data into an actionable target.
SLA: This idx_a677d73c is the external promise at the top of the hierarchy, the most conservative
layer. It's a formal contract with your customers that includes consequences if you fail
•
•
•

85573.title: clouddevopsengineersguide
85573.heading: Chapter 13 234
85573.content:
Chapter 13 234
to meet your objectives. Our pizza service's SLA might be, "If your pizza is not delivered
in under 30 minutes, it's free." An SLA is typically a more lenient version of your SLO,
creating a safety buffer. If your idx_7fcb2121 internal SLO is 99.9% uptime, your external SLA might
be 99.5%, giving you room for unexpected issues without violating customer contracts.
The SLA must be built on proven SLOs; you can't promise customers what you haven't
consistently achieved internally.
This is why hierarchy idx_9f3f5e9c matters; each layer depends on the accuracy and achievement of the
layer below it. You measure SLIs, set internal SLOs based on those measurements, and only
then commit to external SLAs that you're confident you can meet. Violating this hierarchy, for
example, promising customers an SLA without first establishing internal SLOs and reliable SLI
measurements, leads to broken promises and business consequences.
To fully grasp how these three tiers stack together to create a sturdy foundation for your
service commitments, take a look at the hierarchy in the following diagram:
Figure 13.1: A visual aid to understand the hierarchy of SLIs, SLOs, and SLAs
By defining these terms, you move from vague aspirations to a data-driven approach to
reliability. Your SLO becomes the "error budget," the amount of acceptable downtime or
degraded performance. If your SLO is 99.9% uptime, that means you have an error budget of
about 43 minutes of downtime per month. If you are meeting your SLO, you have the "budget"
to take risks, such as rolling out new features. If you are close to violating your SLO, you freeze
new releases and focus all your efforts on improving stability. This creates a powerful feedback
idx_ab7ec390 loop that balances innovation with reliability.
235 System Maintenance and Reliability
Now that you know how to measure and define reliability through SLIs, SLOs, and SLAs, the
next question is: how do you actually build systems that meet these targets? The answer lies in
architecting for failure, that is, designing infrastructure that expects components to break and
continues operating anyway.
High-availability and fault-tolerant architectures
Once you have defined your reliability goals, you can start architecting a system to meet them.
The core principle is to assume that individual components will fail. Servers will crash, disks
will fail, and networks will experience issues. A reliable system is one that is designed to
withstand these failures gracefully. This is achieved through the concepts of High Availability
(HA) and Fault Tolerance (FT). Let's dive deeper into them.
High availability: Surviving failure
HA is about idx_60038cfc minimizing downtime by eliminating single points of failure. The key is
redundancy. Instead of running your application on a single server, you run it on at least two

85574.title: clouddevopsengineersguide
85574.heading: Chapter 13 234
85574.content:
servers behind a load balancer. If one server fails, the load balancer detects this and
automatically redirects all traffic to the remaining healthy server. The service might experience
a brief moment of degraded performance, but it remains available to users.
Think of a hospital that has a backup generator. If the main power grid goes out, there might
be a few seconds where the lights flicker, but then the backup generator kicks in, and the
hospital continues to function. This is HA. The goal isn't to prevent failures entirely, which is
impossible, but rather to ensure that when failures do occur, they don't bring down your entire
system. By maintaining multiple copies of critical components and automatically routing
around failures, HA architectures keep services running even when individual pieces break.
In AWS, the primary tools for achieving HA work together to create a resilient infrastructure
layer. Each tool addresses a specific aspect of availability, from traffic distribution to
geographic redundancy to data persistence. Understanding how these tools complement each
other is essential for building systems that can weather common failure scenarios without
impacting your users.
Let's break down the three core AWS mechanisms that form the foundation of this highly
available architecture:
Elastic Load Balancing (ELB) automatically distributes incoming application traffic
idx_f50c6e2a across idx_c424e190 multiple targets, such as EC2 instances. It acts as the single, stable entry point
for your application. The load balancer continuously performs health checks on your
backend servers, removing unhealthy instances from the rotation and adding them
back once they recover. This automated detection and routing happens in seconds,
ensuring that users are always directed to functioning servers. ELB operates at multiple
•

85575.title: clouddevopsengineersguide
85575.heading: Chapter 13 236
85575.content:
Chapter 13 236
network layers, with ALBs handling HTTP/HTTPS traffic at Layer 7, network load
balancers managing TCP/UDP traffic at Layer 4, and gateway load balancers supporting
third-party virtual appliances.
Multiple Availability Zones (AZs) provide idx_dd57b43d the idx_f8caba05 geographic redundancy necessary for
true HA. An AZ is one or more discrete data centers with redundant power, networking,
and connectivity within an AWS Region. Because they are physically separate, an issue
such as a fire or flood affecting one AZ is unlikely to affect another. By deploying your
resources across multiple AZs, you can protect your application from the failure of an
entire data center. Each AZ is connected to others in the same region through low-
latency, high-bandwidth private networking, allowing your application components to
synchronize data and coordinate operations while remaining physically isolated. This
separation means that common infrastructure failures, such as power outages, cooling
system failures, or network disruptions, that might take down one AZ won't cascade to
affect your other deployments.
Amazon RDS multi-AZ addresses idx_95968a82 the idx_f75bc77c specific challenge of database HA. When you
provision a database with multi-AZ, AWS automatically creates a synchronous standby
replica in a different AZ. If the primary database fails, RDS automatically fails over to
the standby with no data loss, a critical component of any HA database architecture.
The failover process typically completes within 60 to 120 seconds, during which your
application will experience connection errors, but once complete, operations resume
with your data fully intact. RDS handles all the complexity of replication, monitoring,
and failover detection, allowing you to implement database HA without managing the
underlying infrastructure yourself.
While these HA tools idx_6d5cf6a7 ensure your system recovers quickly, accepting brief, manageable
interruptions such as the 60-to-120-second RDS failover, some mission-critical workloads
cannot afford even a single second of downtime. To achieve that absolute level of resilience,
you must move beyond simply recovering from failures and start designing systems that
completely hide them from the user.
Fault tolerance: No interruption
FT is a step idx_625cfb4b beyond HA. It's the ability of a system to continue operating without interruption
when one or more of its components fail. While HA aims to recover quickly, FT aims to have no
user-visible impact at all.
Think of a multi-engine airplane. If one engine fails mid-flight, the plane doesn't fall out of the
sky. The other engines are designed to seamlessly take the extra load, and the flight continues
safely. The passengers might not even know a failure occurred. This is FT. The distinction

85576.title: clouddevopsengineersguide
85576.heading: Chapter 13 236
85576.content:
between HA and FT is crucial: HA accepts brief service degradation during recovery, while FT
•
•
237 System Maintenance and Reliability
demands continuous operation throughout the failure event. This difference has significant
implications for architecture complexity and cost.
Achieving true FT is more complex and expensive than HA. It often involves specialized
hardware and software that can detect a failure and fail over instantaneously. In the cloud, you
can approach FT by using services such as ASGs that can automatically replace failed instances,
and by designing your application to be stateless. ASGs monitor the health of your EC2
instances and automatically launch replacements when failures are detected, maintaining your
desired capacity level. This automated recovery happens continuously in the background,
ensuring that your application always has sufficient healthy instances to handle the workload.
However, the replacement process takes time (typically several minutes to launch and initialize
a new instance), so ASGs alone don't provide instantaneous failover.
A stateless application doesn't idx_d17851fd store any session data on the local server, which means a
user's request can be transparently retried on a different server if the first one fails, without
losing any context. This architectural pattern is fundamental to FT in distributed systems.
When the application state lives in shared external storage such as Amazon ElastiCache,
DynamoDB, or RDS rather than on individual compute instances, those instances become
interchangeable. A request that encounters a failed server can be immediately retried on any
other server in the pool, with the new server accessing the same state data from the shared
storage layer. This approach transforms what would be a visible failure into an invisible
recovery, as users experience nothing more than perhaps a slightly slower response time.
Implementing stateless design requires careful attention to how your application handles
sessions, caches, and temporary data, but the resilience benefits make this investment
worthwhile for systems that require the highest levels of availability.
Now that we've explored the theoretical foundations of HA and FT, it's time to put these
concepts into practice. In the following hands-on exercise, you'll build a self-healing
architecture that demonstrates how these principles work together in real systems.
Hands-on: Building a self-healing system with an
auto-scaling group
This exercise is idx_50fb1f41 about building a classic, robust, and resilient web application architecture on
AWS. Our goal is to create a system that can automatically withstand an instance failure
without any manual intervention and distribute traffic evenly across healthy instances. We
will combine a launch template, an ALB, and an ASG to achieve a truly self-healing system.

85577.title: clouddevopsengineersguide
85577.heading: Chapter 13 236
85577.content:
We will configure the core components for our resilient system. Follow these steps in order to
properly set up the launch template, load balancer, and ASG.

Step 1: Creating a launch template (the instance blueprint)
A launch template is idx_914cdc43 a reusable blueprint that defines the configuration for our EC2 instances.
This ensures that every new instance launched by our ASG is identical. If you have followed
older AWS tutorials, you may have encountered launch configurations, the predecessor to
launch templates. Launch configurations are now deprecated and cannot be used with newer
instance types or features. Always use launch templates for any new work.
Navigate to the EC2 console and select Launch Templates from the left-hand
navigation pane and create a launch template as shown:
Figure 13.2: Create launch template page in the AWS console
Click Create launch template.
Give it idx_a34b3840 a name such as my-app-template and a description.
For Application and OS Images (AMI), choose the Amazon Linux 2 AMI. The user-
data script in this exercise uses the yum package manager, which is correct for Amazon
Linux 2. If you select Amazon Linux 2023, replace yum with dnf in the script, as
Amazon Linux 2023 uses dnf as its default package manager.
For Instance type, select t2.micro (Free Tier-eligible).

Configure it with two inbound rules: one for SSH (port 22) from your IP address to allow for administrative access, and another for HTTP (port 80) from anywhere (0.0.0.0/0) so users and the load balancer can access our web server. Hello from instance $(hostname -f)

" > /usr/share/nginx/html/ index.html This script will idx_4682c828 automatically run when the instance launches, installing an Nginx web server and creating a simple index.html file that displays the instance's unique hostname. Click Create launch template. With our instance blueprint in place, we now need to set up the traffic distribution layer that will route user requests across our instances and monitor their health. Step 2: Creating the load balancer (the traffic cop) The ALB will idx_205a7030 be the single entry point for all user traffic, distributing requests to our backend instances. We'll start by creating a target group, which defines the pool of instances that will receive traffic from the load balancer: In the EC2 console, select Target Groups and click Create target group. Choose Instances as the target type, name it my-app-tg, and keep the protocol as HTTP and port 80.

In the Health checks section, leave the defaults. The ALB will periodically ping the root
path (/) of our instances to ensure the Nginx server is responding correctly. If an
instance fails this check, the ALB will stop sending traffic to it.
Click Next, and then Create target group.
Now, select Load Balancers and click Create Load Balancer.
Choose Application Load Balancer from the load balancer type options.
Name it my-app-alb.

Forward to and choose the my-app-tg target group.

that will maintain our desired instance count and recover from failures.

Step 3: Creating the auto-scaling group (the self-healer)
This is the idx_4f357a28 final piece that brings everything together. The ASG will manage our fleet of
instances.
Let's configure the ASG to use our launch template and connect it to the load balancer we just
created:
In the EC2 console, select Auto Scaling Groups and click Create Auto Scaling group.
Name it my-app-asg.
For Launch template, select the my-app-template template you created in Step 1. Click
Next.
For Network, choose your default VPC and select the same two subnets (in different
AZs) that you chose for your load balancer. Click Next.
For Load balancing, select Attach to an existing load balancer. Choose my-app-tg
from the dropdown. The ASG will now automatically register any instances it launches
with this target group. Enable ELB health checks for added reliability. Click Next.
Group size is where you define the scale. Set Desired capacity to 2, Minimum
capacity to 2, and Maximum capacity to 4. This tells the ASG to always maintain a
fleet of at least two healthy instances, but allows it to scale up to four when demand
increases. To automate this scaling, you would add a scaling policy after creation. A
common and recommended approach is a target tracking policy, for example, keeping
average CPU utilization at 50%. The ASG will then add instances automatically when
load rises and remove them when load drops. You can also pair this with a CloudWatch
alarm, such as an alert that fires when CPU exceeds 70% for two consecutive minutes,
which can trigger the scaling policy or notify your team. This idx_1d7e1268 combination of a scaling
policy and a CloudWatch alarm is how production systems achieve both cost efficiency
and resilience without any manual intervention.
Click through the next steps and finally, select Create Auto Scaling group.
With all three components configured, it's time to see our self-healing architecture in action
and verify that it can automatically recover from instance failures.
Step 4: Verifying and testing the system
The ASG will now idx_4a842474 launch two EC2 instances based on your idx_330874bb launch template. This will take a
few minutes.

85589.title: clouddevopsengineersguide

85589.content:
Chapter 13 242
Let's first confirm that our instances are healthy and the load balancer is distributing traffic
correctly:
Navigate to Target Groups, select my-app-tg, and go to the Targets tab. You should see
two instances, and their status should eventually change to healthy.
Navigate to Load Balancers, select my-app-alb, and copy its DNS name.
Paste the DNS name into your web browser. You should see the message Hello from
instance.... Refresh the page a few times, and you will see the hostname change as the
ALB distributes your requests between the two instances.
Now for the real test: Go to your EC2 instances list. Select one of the instances managed
by the ASG, right-click, and select Terminate instance.
Wait a few minutes. If you watch the Instances screen, you will see the terminated
instance disappear and a brand-new instance being provisioned to replace it. The ASG
detected that the desired capacity (2) was not met and automatically idx_01f0de1b launched a new
instance to self-heal the environment. During this entire process, if you keep refreshing
the idx_e5576581 ALB's DNS name in your browser, your application will remain available, served by
the remaining healthy instance.
You have now successfully built a highly available and self-healing system. It can
automatically recover from common failures and ensures your application remains online and
performant, forming the bedrock of a reliable cloud architecture.

Troubleshooting: Verifying Nginx with curl before checking ALB health
If your instances remain in an unhealthy state for several minutes, SSH into one
of them and confirm that the web server is running locally before relying solely
on the ALB status. Run the following command from inside the instance:
curl localhost
A successful response returns the HTML page with the instance hostname. If
you see no response or a connection error, the user-data script may not have
completed. Check the cloud-init log at /var/log/cloud-init-output.log
for errors, and verify that the security group allows inbound HTTP on port 80.
Note

85591.title: clouddevopsengineersguide
85591.heading: 5.243 System Maintenance and Reliability
85591.content:
5.243 System Maintenance and Reliability
Figure 13.4: ALB in action; same URL, two different hostnames
While the system we just built can handle individual component failures within a region, we
now need to consider what happens when an entire region becomes unavailable due to a major
disaster.
Disaster recovery planning and execution
HA protects idx_8110b795 your application from the failure of a single server or data center. DR, on the other
hand, is about surviving a much larger, catastrophic event, such as the failure of an entire AWS
Region. A good DR plan is like an insurance policy; you hope you never have to use it, but you'll
be glad you have it if you do.
When planning for DR, two metrics are paramount:
Recovery Time Objective (RTO): How idx_8092a73a quickly do you need to be back online after a
disaster is declared? RTO measures the maximum tolerable downtime for your
application. For a critical e-commerce platform, your RTO might be 15 minutes,
meaning every minute of downtime beyond that threshold represents unacceptable
revenue loss and customer impact. For an internal reporting tool, an RTO of 24 hours
might be perfectly reasonable. RTO directly influences your infrastructure costs
because faster recovery requires more resources to be provisioned and standing by in
your recovery region.
Recovery Point Objective (RPO): How idx_160535ef much data can you afford to lose? RPO
measures the maximum acceptable age of data that might be lost in a disaster. If your
RPO is five minutes, you need a replication strategy that ensures data written more
than five minutes ago is safely stored in your recovery location. For financial
transactions, you might require an RPO of near-zero (seconds), necessitating
synchronous replication. For analytics data that can be regenerated, an RPO of 24 hours
using nightly backups might suffice. RPO determines your backup frequency and
replication strategy, with tighter RPOs requiring more sophisticated and expensive
solutions.
•
•

85592.title: clouddevopsengineersguide
85592.heading: Chapter 13 244
85592.content:
Chapter 13 244
The answers idx_5034dcd9 to these questions will determine which DR strategy is right for you, as each one
represents a different trade-off between cost and recovery time. The most common strategies
on AWS are as follows:
Backup and restore: This is idx_cd0ac627 the simplest and most cost-effective strategy. You
regularly back up your data (e.g., RDS snapshots and EBS snapshots) to another region.
In a disaster, you would manually provision a new environment in the recovery region
and restore your data from these backups. This is suitable for non-critical systems
where an RTO of several hours is acceptable.
Pilot light: A idx_f1db63e3 small core of your infrastructure is always running in the recovery region.
For example, your database might be replicated, but your application servers are
turned off. In a disaster, you would "light" the pilot by starting up the application
servers and scaling out the infrastructure. This offers a much faster RTO (minutes
instead of hours) and is a good balance for business-critical applications.
Warm standby: A idx_b5c20919 scaled-down but fully functional version of your environment is
always running in the recovery region. It can handle a small amount of traffic. In a
disaster, you would redirect all traffic to the standby region and quickly scale it up to
handle the full production load. This provides an even faster RTO and is often used for
core business systems.
Multi-site active-active: This is idx_ae65c311 the most resilient and most expensive strategy. You
run your full application stack in two or more regions simultaneously, and traffic is
distributed between them using a service such as Amazon Route 53. If one region fails,
the other region is already handling a portion of the load and can be scaled to absorb
the rest. This can achieve a near-zero RTO and RPO, and is reserved for mission-critical
services where any downtime is unacceptable. Route 53 makes this strategy practical
through two complementary features. First, Route 53 health checks continuously probe
your application endpoints in each region. If an endpoint stops responding, Route 53
marks it as unhealthy and stops routing traffic to it. Second, with failover routing
policies, you can designate one region as the primary and another as the secondary, so
traffic automatically shifts to the secondary when the primary health check fails. For a
true active-active setup, a weighted or latency-based routing policy distributes
requests across both regions simultaneously, with Route 53 removing a region from
rotation the moment its health check fails. This combination gives you automatic,
DNS-level failover with no manual intervention required.
Let's consider a idx_43e458c6 real-world scenario of an online banking platform that processes thousands of

85593.title: clouddevopsengineersguide
85593.heading: Chapter 13 244
85593.content:
transactions per minute. The business determines that any downtime during trading hours
could result in significant financial losses and regulatory penalties, establishing an RTO of five
minutes. Since every transaction represents actual money movement, they cannot afford to
•
•
•
•
245 System Maintenance and Reliability
lose any completed transactions, setting an RPO of 30 seconds. These strict requirements push
them toward a warm standby strategy with continuous database replication to a secondary
region. The additional infrastructure costs are justified by the potential losses from extended
downtime, and monthly DR drills ensure the team can execute the failover procedure
confidently within their five-minute window.
Having established how to protect against catastrophic regional failures, you now have a
complete picture of system reliability, from handling individual component failures through
HA to surviving region-wide disasters through DR.
Testing your DR plan regularly is non-negotiable. A DR plan that has never been tested is
merely a document, not a working strategy. Schedule DR drills at least annually, where you
simulate a regional failure and execute your recovery procedures. These tests will reveal gaps in
your runbooks, expose dependencies you didn't know existed, and train your team to respond
effectively under pressure. AWS services such as AWS Backup and AWS Elastic Disaster
Recovery can automate much of this testing, making it easier to validate that your RTO and
RPO targets are achievable in practice.
Summary
In this chapter, you learned how to build systems that maintain reliability in production. You
started by mastering the professional language of reliability engineering, understanding how
SLIs provide raw measurements, SLOs set internal targets, and SLAs formalize external
promises to customers. This hierarchy taught you to quantify reliability and manage it through
error budgets that balance innovation with stability.
You explored architectural patterns for resilience, distinguishing between HA, which
minimizes downtime through redundancy and quick recovery, and FT, which aims for zero
user-visible impact during failures. You learned how AWS services such as ELB, multi-AZ
deployments, and stateless application design create systems that expect components to fail
yet continue operating.
The hands-on exercise brought these concepts to life as you built a self-healing architecture
using a launch template, ALB, and ASG. You witnessed how a properly configured system
automatically detects failed instances, removes them from service, and launches replacements
without manual intervention.
Finally, you examined DR planning for catastrophic events such as regional failures. By
understanding RTO and RPO, you learned how to select appropriate DR strategies, from simple

85594.title: clouddevopsengineersguide
85594.heading: Chapter 13 244
85594.content:
backup-and-restore to sophisticated multi-region active-active deployments, and why
regularly testing DR procedures is essential.

learning how to identify bottlenecks, use feedback loops, and manage your cloud spend

You have reached the pinnacle of modern software delivery. You have a fast, automated CI/CD
pipeline; a secure, observable, and highly reliable production environment; and the skills to
manage the entire lifecycle from a developer's first line of code to a globally available
application. Your software factory is fully operational. But a new, more strategic challenge now
presents itself: How do we make the factory better? How do we make it faster, more efficient,
and more cost-effective? A functional system is a great achievement, but a truly excellent
DevOps practice is one that never stops improving.
This chapter is about optimization and sustainability. It's about taking the powerful systems
you've built and fine-tuning them for peak performance and financial efficiency. We will begin
by learning how to analyze your CI/CD pipeline to identify and remove bottlenecks that slow
down your development velocity. You'll learn how to create powerful feedback loops that use
data from production to inform and improve the development process. You will then get
hands-on with a critical aspect of modern cloud operations: cost management, learning how
to implement monitoring and alerts to prevent budget overruns. We'll explore powerful
strategies for reducing your cloud spend and, finally, discuss how to foster a culture of
continuous improvement that makes optimization a natural part of your team's DNA.
In this chapter, we're going to cover the following main topics:
Identifying and removing bottlenecks in your pipeline
Using feedback loops for process optimization
Hands-on: Implementing cloud cost monitoring and alerts
Strategies for reducing cloud spend
Fostering a culture of continuous improvement

Technical requirements
The hands-on exercise in this chapter requires an active AWS account. You will need IAM
permissions to access and use the AWS Billing and Cost Management console, specifically,
services such as AWS Cost Explorer and AWS Budgets. While the Free Tier is sufficient, having
some minor resource usage from previous chapters will make the Cost Explorer data more

85596.heading: Chapter 13 246
85596.content:

the Download the example code files section in the Preface of this book.

Identifying and removing bottlenecks in your
pipeline
Your CI/CD pipeline is idx_1b0d5ce1 the central artery of your development process. Its efficiency idx_f08fc780 directly
impacts how quickly you can deliver value to your users. A bottleneck is any stage in your
pipeline that slows down the entire process, just idx_b9ad9f13 like a single closed lane on a highway can
cause miles of traffic jams. Identifying and eliminating these bottlenecks is one of the most
impactful ways to improve your team's velocity.
The first step is to measure everything. You cannot optimize what you cannot measure. Most
modern CI/CD platforms, including GitHub Actions and AWS CodePipeline, provide detailed
metrics on the idx_b960c8fc execution of your workflows. You should be tracking a few key performance
indicators (KPIs) for idx_f942d3f5 your pipeline:
Pipeline lead time: The total time from a code commit to a successful production
deployment. This is your most important high-level metric.
Build duration: The time it takes for your "build and test" stage to complete. This is
often the longest and most resource-intensive part of the pipeline.
Deployment frequency: How often you are successfully deploying to production. Elite
DevOps teams deploy multiple times per day.
Change failure rate: The percentage of deployments that result in a production failure
(e.g., requiring a rollback or a hotfix).
By analyzing these metrics, you can start to pinpoint your biggest constraints. Is the total lead
time long because the build itself takes 45 minutes? Or is the build fast, but the code then sits
for days waiting for a manual QA or approval process?
•
•
•
•

85597.title: clouddevopsengineersguide
85597.heading: Chapter 14 250
85597.content:
Chapter 14 250
Once you've identified where delays are occurring through your metrics, you can apply
targeted solutions to the most common problem areas that slow down delivery.
Common bottlenecks and how to fix them
While every system is unique, several common bottlenecks appear in many CI/CD pipelines.
Slow build and test idx_84bb316f stages are perhaps the most frequent culprits. As a code base grows, the
time it takes to compile the code and run the entire test suite can balloon, stretching a 5-
minute build into a 50-minute marathon. This is a major drag on productivity. The idx_7beee027 primary
solution is parallelization. Break your monolithic test suite into smaller, independent chunks
(e.g., unit tests, integration tests, and end-to-end tests) and run them simultaneously on
multiple build agents. Another key idx_b36db444 strategy is caching. Your build process often downloads the
same dependencies over and over again. By caching these dependencies (such as Node.js
modules, Maven packages, or Docker layers) between pipeline runs, you can save a significant
amount of time.
Manual handoffs and approval gates are another idx_3d38e0e6 common source of delay. If your idx_6c1f3e7d pipeline
requires a developer to manually hand off a build to a QA engineer, who then runs tests and
hands it off to an operations person for deployment, you are introducing significant idle time.
The goal is to automate as much as possible. For approvals that must remain manual (such as a
product manager signing off on a feature before a production release), ensure that the process
is streamlined. The pipeline should automatically send a notification to the approver with all
the necessary context, and the approval should be a simple, one-click action that allows the
pipeline to proceed.
Flaky tests are idx_0e9227b8 a more insidious bottleneck. These are tests that sometimes pass and
sometimes fail for the same code, often due to issues such as timing or reliance on external
services. A flaky test that fails can halt the entire pipeline, forcing a developer to investigate
and rerun the job, wasting valuable time and eroding trust in the test suite. It is critical to have
a process for identifying and either fixing or removing these non-deterministic tests.
Use case: Speeding up a slow e-commerce pipeline
Consider the idx_e4a44e04 case of an e-commerce start-up that was struggling with deployment speed.
Their development team wanted to push bug fixes and new features quickly to stay
competitive during peak shopping seasons, but their CI/CD pipeline was taking over two hours
from commit to production. Customer complaints about checkout issues were piling up, and
fixes were taking far too long to reach users.
After instrumenting their pipeline with detailed metrics, the team discovered their main

85598.title: clouddevopsengineersguide
85598.heading: Chapter 14 250
85598.content:
bottleneck was in the build and test stage, which was consuming 90 minutes of the total
pipeline time. Digging deeper, they found that their end-to-end test suite was running all 500
251 Continuous Improvement and Cost Optimization
tests sequentially on a single build agent, including tests for features unrelated to the changes
being deployed.
The team implemented three key optimizations:
First, they parallelized their test suite across multiple build agents, splitting tests into
four groups that ran simultaneously.
Second, they implemented intelligent test selection that only ran tests relevant to the
changed code for non-production branches.
Third, they moved their Docker image builds to use layer caching, which prevented
rebuilding unchanged dependencies on every run.
The results idx_c2bb2952 were dramatic. Their pipeline lead time dropped from 2 hours to just 25 minutes,
an 80% improvement. Deployment frequency increased from twice per week to multiple times
per day. More importantly, when a critical payment processing bug was discovered during
Black Friday, they were able to push a fix to production in under 30 minutes instead of the 2+
hours it would have taken previously. This single improvement potentially saved hundreds of
thousands in lost revenue during their busiest shopping day of the year.
Once you've optimized your pipeline's speed and efficiency, the next step is to ensure that the
data flowing through it actively improves your development process over time.
Using feedback loops for process optimization
A CI/CD pipeline idx_32b62982 is not just a one-way street for shipping code. It is the engine of a powerful
feedback loop that connects your developers directly to the operational reality of your
production environment. The data and insights generated by your running application are a
goldmine. Using this feedback to inform the development process is the key to creating a
learning organization that gets progressively better over time.
The concept of feedback loops in software development mirrors the scientific method: you
form a hypothesis (write code), run an experiment (deploy it), observe the results (monitor
production), and use those observations to inform your next hypothesis. Without these
feedback mechanisms, teams are essentially flying blind, making decisions based on
assumptions rather than evidence. The organizations that excel at DevOps are those that have
built tight, effective feedback loops at every stage of their delivery process.
Types of feedback
Effective idx_d7d8d5d1 feedback loops operate on different timescales and provide different kinds of
information. Each type serves a distinct purpose in the development life cycle, and together
they create a comprehensive system for continuous learning and improvement.

85600.title: clouddevopsengineersguide
85600.heading: Chapter 14 252
85600.content:
Chapter 14 252
The developer feedback loop is idx_c2022bb6 the fastest and tightest loop, operating idx_e349f543 on a timescale of
minutes. When a developer commits a piece of code, they need to know as quickly as possible if
it broke anything. This is the primary job of your CI stage. The build should run automatically,
and if it fails, the developer should receive an immediate notification in their primary
communication tool, such as Slack or directly within the GitHub pull request. A feedback loop
that takes idx_13f3815d hours is ineffective; the goal is to provide feedback in minutes, while the code is still
fresh in the developer's mind. The idx_f39533cb psychology here matters tremendously. When feedback
arrives within 5 to 10 minutes, the developer still has the full context of their changes loaded in
their mental workspace. They can quickly identify and fix issues without the cognitive
overhead of context-switching. However, when feedback arrives hours later, the developer has
moved on to other tasks, and returning to fix the problem requires significant mental effort to
rebuild that context. This is why optimizing your build and test speed, as discussed earlier,
directly impacts the quality of this feedback loop.
The application performance feedback loop operates idx_e2e538eb on a idx_81bcecac timescale of hours to days and
uses the observability tools we discussed in Chapter 10. Data from your application
performance monitoring (APM) tools, such idx_867c310b as traces showing slow database queries or
metrics showing high memory usage for a particular service, should not just be used for
incident response. This data should be systematically fed back into the development backlog.
Your team can then prioritize work on performance improvements and technical debt based on
real-world production data, not just guesswork. For example, if your APM tools reveal that 30%
of all requests to your API are hitting a particular endpoint that consistently takes over two
seconds to respond, this becomes a clear, data-driven candidate for optimization work.
Without this feedback loop, teams often waste time optimizing parts of the system that aren't
actually causing problems, while real bottlenecks go unaddressed. The key is to establish
regular cadences where the team reviews production metrics together, perhaps in weekly
technical health reviews, and translates those insights into actionable backlog items with clear
business justification.
The user feedback loop connects idx_a4b0c0ef your users' experience directly to the idx_bf235662 code and operates on a
timescale of days to weeks. When a user reports a bug through a customer support channel,
that ticket should be linked back to the specific release and, if possible, the exact commits that
introduced the issue. This creates a clear, traceable path from user impact back to the source,

85601.title: clouddevopsengineersguide
85601.heading: Chapter 14 252
85601.content:
enabling faster fixes and a deeper understanding of how your code affects your customers.
Modern incident management tools can automatically correlate error reports with deployment
events, helping you quickly identify whether a recent release introduced a regression. Beyond
bug reports, this loop should also include positive signals. If a new feature launches and you
see a spike in user engagement or conversion rates, that success should be communicated back
to the development team. This reinforcement helps teams understand what kinds of changes
create real value and encourages more of that work. Many high-performing teams display real-
253 Continuous Improvement and Cost Optimization
time user metrics on dashboards visible to all engineers, creating a constant ambient
awareness of how their work impacts the business.
Implementing effective feedback mechanisms
Building idx_eef45524 these feedback loops requires both technical infrastructure and organizational
discipline. On the technical side, you need automated systems that capture the right data at
each stage and present it in actionable ways. This means integrating your CI/CD pipeline with
your monitoring systems, your issue tracking tools, and your communication platforms. For
instance, when a deployment completes, your pipeline should automatically trigger a
comparison of key metrics before and after the deployment, alerting the team if error rates
spike or performance degrades.
On the organizational side, you need to create a culture where feedback is not just collected but
actually acted upon. This means establishing clear processes for triaging issues identified
through feedback loops, dedicating time in your sprint planning for addressing technical debt
revealed by production metrics, and celebrating when feedback leads to meaningful
improvements. Teams that excel at this often have "you build it, you run it" policies where
developers are on-call for the services they create, ensuring that they experience firsthand the
operational consequences of their code decisions. This direct accountability creates the
strongest possible feedback loop.
While feedback loops help you optimize your technical processes, one of the most important
metrics to monitor in cloud environments is cost, which can spiral unexpectedly without
proper visibility and alerting.
Hands-on: Implementing cloud cost monitoring and
alerts
One idx_b94de06c of the most critical feedback loops in the cloud era is cost. The pay-as-you-go model of the
cloud is incredibly powerful, but it can also idx_3921dd1f lead to bill shock, a surprisingly large bill at the
end of the month caused by forgotten resources or unexpected usage. The first step to
managing cost is gaining visibility. In this exercise, we will use AWS's native tools to explore

85602.title: clouddevopsengineersguide
85602.heading: Chapter 14 252
85602.content: our spending and set up a budget alert to act as an early warning system.

Step 1: Gaining visibility with AWS Cost Explorer
AWS Cost Explorer is idx_293bb67f a free tool that idx_64c68b77 provides a detailed, interactive interface for viewing and
analyzing your costs and usage. Before you can use it, you must enable it. After clicking Enable,
AWS needs time to process and prepare your historical billing data, so the dashboard may not
be immediately available and can take up to 24 hours to populate. Once active, Cost Explorer
shows costs aggregated across all AWS regions by default. To isolate spending in a specific
region, use the Region filter in the Filters panel on the right side of the dashboard.
Let's walk through idx_b35de841 enabling Cost Explorer idx_e0fec48f and performing your first cost analysis:
First, navigate to the idx_84d4496b main AWS Management Console. In the search bar at the top,
type Billing and select Billing & Cost Management from the results. This will take
you to your central hub for all financial information related to your AWS account.
In the left-hand navigation pane, find and click on Cost Explorer. If you've never used
it before, you will see a welcome screen. Click the button to enable Cost Explorer.
Figure 14.1: Cost Explorer overview
Once enabled (which may take a day), the main dashboard gives you a high-level
overview of your current month's spending. On the right-hand side, you'll see a panel
with a set of filters. This is where the real power of the tool lies.
Let's perform a simple analysis. Find the Group by filter and select Service. The chart
will instantly update to show you a breakdown of your spending by each AWS service

85604.content:

(e.g., EC2, S3, and RDS). This is the first and most important question to answer: where
is my money going? You might be surprised to see which services are contributing the
most to your bill.
Figure 14.2: Selecting a Cost filter from the side menu
Now, let's try idx_d517702c another idx_dbce130a powerful filter. In the Group by dropdown, clear the Service
selection and choose Tag. If you have been tagging your resources (as we did in
previous chapters, for example, Env:Staging), a new dropdown will appear. Select
your tag key (e.g., Env). The chart will now group all costs by the values of that tag. This
allows you to answer critical business questions, such as, How much is our staging
environment costing us versus our production environment? This is the foundation of
Financial Operations (FinOPs), which is the idx_065edc68 practice of bringing financial
accountability to the variable spend model of the cloud.

For tag-based cost grouping to be idx_386cdfed meaningful, tagging must be applied consistently across all
resources. A resource that lacks the expected tag simply does not appear in the filtered view,
which can skew your analysis. If you are operating within AWS Organizations, you can enforce
tagging at scale using tag policies, which define which tag keys and values are acceptable and
can prevent the creation of non-compliant resources. Even outside of Organizations,
establishing a mandatory tagging strategy from the start, covering dimensions such as
environment, team, and project, will pay dividends as your infrastructure grows and cost

With cost visibility established, the next step is setting up proactive alerts to catch spending
issues before they become problems.
Step 2: Creating your first budget
Now that we can idx_ea7d2861 see our historical and current costs, let's create a proactive monitor to prevent
future surprises. AWS Budgets allows you to set custom cost and usage budgets that notify you
when you exceed (or are forecasted to exceed) your defined thresholds.
Follow these steps to create a simple monthly budget with email notifications:
In the Billing console, under Budgets and Planning, in the left-hand navigation, click
on Budgets.
Click the Create budget button.
On the Choose budget type screen, you have several options. For our purpose, choose
Use a template (simplified).
For the template type, select Monthly cost budget.
Now, you'll configure the budget details. Give your budget a descriptive name, such as
monthly-total-spend.
For the budgeted amount, it's important to start with a realistic but low number for a

Add the email where you want to receive the notification; you can add more than one

Leave the budget scope as All AWS services for now and click Next.

85608.content:
7.8 257 Continuous Improvement and Cost Optimization
Figure 14.3: The Create Budget page overview
Your budget is idx_3b180f1d now active and will monitor your spending continuously throughout the
month.
You have now created a critical financial safety net. If your AWS spending in a given month
exceeds $10, you will automatically receive an email alert. This simple mechanism is one of the
most effective ways to prevent unexpected costs and maintain financial control over your cloud
environment.
Having established visibility and alerting, you're now ready to take action on reducing your
actual cloud spending through targeted optimization strategies.
Beyond reactive budgets, AWS also provides two complementary tools that add a proactive
layer to cost management. The first is forecasting, built directly into Cost Explorer. Once you
have several months of billing history, Cost Explorer projects your end-of-month spend based
on current trends, giving you an early signal of whether you are on track to stay within budget
before the month closes. The idx_6a24e1fd second is AWS Cost Anomaly Detection, a service that uses
machine learning to establish a baseline of your normal spending patterns and automatically
alerts you when it detects an unusual spike. Unlike a budget threshold, which is a static dollar
value you set manually, anomaly detection adapts to your usage over time and can flag
unexpected increases in a specific service or linked account before they accumulate into a large

85609.title: clouddevopsengineersguide
85609.heading: Chapter 14 258
85609.content:
Chapter 14 258
bill. Enabling both forecasting and anomaly detection alongside your budget alerts forms a
complete early warning system for cloud costs.
Strategies for reducing cloud spend
Once you have idx_db3701f7 visibility and alerts in place, you can move on to active cost optimization.
There are numerous strategies for reducing your cloud bill, but they idx_2089b91b generally fall into a few
key categories:
Right-sizing resources is often the easiest win. It's very common for developers to
provision servers that are much larger than they need, "just in case." This is like buying
a 10-bedroom house for a family of two. AWS provides tools such as AWS Compute
Optimizer that use machine learning to analyze the actual CPU and memory usage of
your instances and recommend a more appropriately sized (and cheaper) instance type.
Choosing the right purchasing model is critical for long-running workloads. Running
everything on On-Demand Instances is the most expensive option. If you have a
predictable, steady-state workload (such as a production web server), you can achieve
significant savings (up to 72%) by using AWS Savings Plans or Reserved Instances.
These are like making a 1- or 3-year commitment to a certain amount of compute usage
in exchange for a steep discount. For workloads that are fault-tolerant and can be
interrupted, such as CI/CD build agents or data processing jobs, you can use EC2 Spot
Instances, which allow you to bid on spare EC2 capacity for savings of up to 90%.
Storage optimization is another key area. Storing data in the standard S3 tier can
become expensive for large datasets that are not accessed frequently. You can use S3
lifecycle policies to automatically transition data to cheaper storage tiers, such as S3
Infrequent Access or S3 Glacier, after a certain period.
Automating shutdowns is a simple but highly effective strategy. Non-production
environments, such as development and staging, often only need to be running during
business hours. By creating a simple scheduled script (using AWS Lambda and
EventBridge) to shut these environments down every evening and on weekends, you
can often cut their costs by more than 50%.
While each of these strategies can deliver savings individually, their real power emerges when
applied together as part of a comprehensive optimization approach.
Use case: A media company cuts cloud costs by 60%
A digital media idx_7f4ff6b8 company with a growing video streaming platform was facing escalating AWS
bills that threatened its profitability. Their monthly costs had climbed to $45,000, with most of
the spending concentrated in compute and storage. The engineering team knew they needed to
optimize, but weren't sure where to start.
•
•
•
•
259 Continuous Improvement and Cost Optimization
After implementing Cost Explorer and analyzing their spending patterns, they discovered

85610.title: clouddevopsengineersguide
85610.heading: Chapter 14 258
85610.content:
several optimization opportunities. Their most significant finding was that they were running
15 large EC2 instances (m5.2xlarge) for their web application tier 24/7, but CPU utilization
averaged only 15%. Using AWS Compute Optimizer's recommendations, they right-sized these
instances to m5.large, immediately reducing compute costs by 50% for that workload.
Next, they tackled their idx_cf1907b3 development and staging environments, which were running
continuously even though developers only worked business hours. They implemented
automated shutdown schedules using Lambda functions, saving an additional $8,000 per
month by having these environments active only 23% of the time instead of 100%.
For their production workload, they switched from On-Demand Instances to a 1-year Savings
Plan, achieving a 40% discount while keeping some On-Demand capacity for traffic spikes.
Finally, they implemented S3 lifecycle policies to automatically move older videos to cheaper
storage tiers, reducing storage costs by 70% for archived content.
The combined impact reduced their monthly AWS bill from $45,000 to $18,000, a 60%
reduction that saved over $300,000 annually. They established ongoing cost governance
practices with weekly Cost Explorer reviews and quarterly optimization sprints, ensuring that
costs remained under control as they continued to grow.
These cost optimization strategies work hand in hand with the performance and reliability
practices we've covered throughout this book, demonstrating that efficient systems are not just
faster and more reliable, but also more economical to operate.
Fostering a culture of continuous improvement
Ultimately, DevOps is idx_29cf2f90 not just a set of tools or a technical process; it's a culture. The most
successful DevOps organizations are those that embrace a culture of continuous improvement,
often referred to by the Japanese term Kaizen. The goal is to create an environment where
everyone on the team feels empowered and responsible for making the system better every
single day.
This culture is built on a foundation of a few key practices:
Blameless post-mortem: When an incident occurs, and they will, the goal is not to
find someone to blame. The goal is to conduct a detailed analysis to understand the
systemic causes of the failure. What was the technical root cause? What part of our
process allowed this to happen? What can we do to prevent this entire class of
problems from happening again? The output of a post-mortem is a set of concrete
action items for improvement.
•

85611.title: clouddevopsengineersguide
85611.heading: Chapter 14 260
85611.content:
Chapter 14 260
Regular retrospective: At the end of a sprint or a project, the team gets together to
discuss three simple questions: What went well? What didn't go well? And what will
we do differently next time? This creates a structured, safe environment for the team to
reflect on its processes and identify small, incremental improvements.
DevOps culture: The management must support a culture in which teams are given
the time and resources to act on the improvements they identify. This often means
formally allocating a portion of the team's capacity (e.g., 20% of each sprint) to
"improvement work," such as paying down technical debt, improving the CI/CD
pipeline, or automating a manual task. By making improvement a formal part of the
job, you create a powerful virtuous cycle where the system, the processes, and the team
get progressively better over time.
With a solid understanding idx_46cc931d of continuous improvement practices, technical optimization
strategies, and cost management techniques, you now have all the essential tools needed to
build and maintain high-performing DevOps systems.
Summary
In this chapter, you learned how to take your functional DevOps practice and make it truly
efficient and sustainable. You learned how to analyze your CI/CD pipeline to identify and
eliminate bottlenecks, increasing your development velocity. You explored the power of
feedback loops, using production data to drive improvements in development. You got hands-
on with cloud financial management, using AWS Cost Explorer and AWS Budgets to gain
visibility into your spending and create a crucial alerting safety net.
We then discussed powerful strategies for actively reducing your cloud spend, from right-
sizing instances to choosing the right purchasing models. Finally, and most importantly, you
learned that continuous improvement is a cultural practice, built on blameless post-mortems,
regular retrospectives, and a commitment to making things better every day.
You have now completed the journey through the core principles and practices of modern
DevOps. You have the skills to build, deploy, secure, observe, and optimize a complete software
system. In the final part of this book, we will look to the horizon, exploring the emerging
trends that are shaping the future of DevOps and providing guidance on how to build a
successful career in this exciting and ever-evolving field.
